Yes. 

The manipulation of time in the story is exceptionally well-balanced and serves the quiet, melancholic mood of the narrative. 

At the beginning, the author stretches time slightly: the simple act of unlocking a door and standing on the doormat is drawn out through muscle memory, sensory details (the cold), and Judith's visual inventory of the hallway, which triggers childhood memories and a brief flashback to a phone call with the notary. This slowing down of time effectively mirrors Judith's hesitation and the heavy silence of the empty house. 

Conversely, the author uses time compression effectively in the second half. Rather than narrating every step of Judith's search through the house, the move from the kitchen on the ground floor to the linen closet upstairs is compressed into a single transition ("Im Wäscheschrank oben fand sie die Frucht schließlich doch..."). Months of the house standing empty ("Seit dem März... der Oktober") and a lifetime of her mother's habits are also compressed into single sentences. This keeps the short story focused tightly on the central emotional mystery—the quince—before slowing back down at the end as Judith sits on the bed, leaving the reader in a lingering, contemplative moment.
